question: Can a bulk-and-spike Hessian spectrum arise in a deep network even when the data covariance is spectrally balanced, and under what deep-linear assumptions does the dominant-to-bulk curvature gap scale with network depth?

key_findings.claim: A clean special-case algebraic result is present: at uniform rank-r balanced factors, the outer-product/Gauss-Newton Hessian has one eigenvalue level L times another even though the active data covariance is isotropic.
key_findings.evidence: With sufficient hidden width, aligned rank-r target cross-covariance, and Uniform Spectral Initialization Sigma_0^(1/L)=mu I_r, Lemma A.1 diagonalizes A_o^T A_o in the u_i tensor v_j basis. It obtains L mu^(2(L-1)) with multiplicity r^2 and mu^(2(L-1)) with multiplicity (d_0+d_L-2r)r. This establishes an architecture-induced two-level nonzero spectrum for the Gauss-Newton part under stronger assumptions than the general theorem states.

key_findings.claim: The general Theorem 3.5 claims r^2 dominant eigenvalues of scale L m_t^(2(L-1)), a bulk of scale m_t^(2(L-1)), and asymptotically negligible remaining curvature, but its proof does not cover its stated initialization class.
key_findings.evidence: The theorem assumes only Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 and controls the first r factor singular values. Lemma A.9, which supplies the spectrum, additionally sets Sigma_t^(1/L)=diag(lambda_1,...,lambda_r,0,...,0). That zero initialization outside the target rank follows from Assumption 3.3 but is absent from Theorem 3.5. With nonzero unused singular values, Appendix Lemma A.2 instead gives lambda_{i,t+1}=lambda_{i,t}-eta lambda_{i,t}^{2L-1}; those modes remain nonzero at finite t and contribute extra Hessian eigenvalues.

key_findings.claim: The paper uses mutually incompatible dynamics for the d_*-r singular modes and mutually incompatible covariance ranks, so the exponential perturbation argument cannot be accepted as written.
key_findings.evidence: Main-text Lemma 3.4 and the repeated lemma on pages 23-24 say modes i>r remain at initialization. Lemmas A.2-A.3 derive that they decay toward zero. Lemmas A.7-A.8 again say they remain fixed and do not affect loss. The source is a silent change from main Assumption 3.1, Sigma_xx approximately I_{d_*}, to Sigma_xx approximately I_r in several appendix proofs; under I_{d_*}, unused target modes receive the decay update, whereas under rank-r covariance they can be unobserved. For L>1 the displayed decay recurrence is polynomial near zero, not the exponential O(exp(-L alpha eta t)) used for the claimed zero space.

anchors.section: Lemma A.7, treatment of inactive modes

key_findings.claim: The stated zero-space multiplicity counts zeros of the d_L d_0 Gram matrix, not all eigenvalues of the full parameter Hessian.
key_findings.evidence: The proof transfers nonzero eigenvalues from H_o=A_o A_o^T to A_o^T A_o, whose dimension is d_L d_0, then reports (d_L-r)(d_0-r) zeros as if that completed the spectrum of H_o. A deep network has P=sum_l d_l d_{l-1} parameters and therefore H_o has at least P-(d_0+d_L-r)r zero eigenvalues. In the main L=3 simulation, d_0=10, d_1=d_2=20, d_L=16, and r=4 give P=920 and 88 predicted nonzeros, hence 832 outer-product null directions, not the 72 zeros obtained inside the 160-dimensional Gram matrix. At finite loss the functional Hessian can also perturb additional parameter directions, so the full-Hessian 'remaining eigenvalues' require a separate count.

key_findings.claim: The separation condition is described backwards and does not by itself prove a uniform Theta(L) gap.
key_findings.evidence: The threshold L^(1/(2(L-1))) decreases toward one as depth grows (for example, from sqrt(2) at L=2 to about 1.176 at L=7), so for a fixed relative singular-value spread the condition becomes more stringent, contrary to the page-6 remark that it becomes easier with depth. In the theorem proof, the condition only gives q^(2(L-1))<L for q=(m+delta)/(m-delta); substituting this into the displayed ratio bounds allows an upper order L^2 and a lower order one, not constants times L uniformly. The exact L ratio is valid in the uniform-spectrum special case or asymptotically after an additional q-to-one argument.

key_findings.claim: For the true Hessian, the paper establishes at most convergence of the nonzero ratio toward L in the uniform case, not an exactly L finite-time ratio.
key_findings.evidence: The Gauss-Newton/outer-product levels have exact ratio L when all active singular values equal mu_t. The full Hessian adds a functional term bounded as O(exp(-L alpha eta t)). Corollary 3.6 nevertheless states lambda_dom/lambda_bulk=L, while its appendix proof obtains L+O(exp(-L alpha eta t)) and says the ratio converges to L. Perturbations can also split repeated eigenvalues, so 'exactly two distinct nonzero eigenvalues up to a perturbation' is only an asymptotic cluster statement.

key_findings.claim: The functional-Hessian decay proof has an additional loss-definition gap: it alternates among pointwise loss, population loss, and excess loss.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma A.6 starts from L_W(x,y)<epsilon but then bounds the expected residual and functional Hessian. Lemma A.7 allows irreducible population loss L_min=E||y||^2/2-r/2 and proves exponential decay only for the excess loss. Lemma A.8 plugs that excess decay into the Lemma A.6 square-root bound while describing epsilon as population excess loss, although Lemma A.6 was written for the uncentered residual loss. Directly controlling Omega may repair the argument under the aligned moment model, but that repair is not supplied.

anchors.section: Lemma A.6 proof and Lemma A.7
Lemma A.7, L_min and excess loss

key_findings.claim: The synthetic deep-linear experiment matches the intended special case: for L=3 and rank 4, 16 dominant and 72 bulk eigenvalues separate with a mean gap near three while the training loss converges.
key_findings.evidence: The main experiment uses input dimension 10, output dimension 16, two hidden widths of 20, rank 4, whitened population moments, and balanced aligned initialization. Figure 2 plots the Hessian trajectories and loss; the reported multiplicities r^2=16 and (d_*+d_L-2r)r=72 agree here because d_*=d_0=10. Figure 1 also plots depths 2-7 and reports the empirical mean dominant-to-bulk ratio tracking Gap=L.

key_findings.claim: A tanh simulation suggests, but does not establish, extension beyond deep linear networks.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 3 repeats the small synthetic setup with tanh after each layer and shows a visually separated nonzero spectrum for L=3 and mean gaps that track L for depths 2-7. There is no nonlinear theorem, no ReLU/residual/convolutional experiment, no natural dataset, no optimizer variation, and no uncertainty over seeds. Saturation, width scaling, target rank, and normalization can all alter the nonlinear Hessian.

anchors.section: 4, Discussion Beyond Theoretical Setup and Figure 3

key_findings.claim: The 14-page simulation appendix is a rank/depth visualization rather than a documented robustness study, and its repeated captions contain concrete labeling errors.
key_findings.evidence: Rendered pages 28-41 show paired depth panels L=2-4 and L=5-7 while every caption says the panels are L=3, L=4, and L=5. The legends progress from r^2=16 through 100, consistent with ranks 4-10, but the captions claim dominant plus bulk always equals input dimension times output dimension; for rank 4 the displayed nonzero count is 88, not 160, and equality holds only at full rank 10. No surrounding text specifies what varies, the sample count, learning rate, initialization draw, repetitions, or numeric gap table.

key_findings.claim: The work gives an existence counterexample to 'data imbalance is necessary' under a highly aligned active subspace, but it does not show that depth is the dominant source of spikes in ordinary deep networks.
key_findings.evidence: The data covariance is isotropic on its padded support, but the target cross-covariance U I_r V^T is rank deficient when r<d_* and is exactly aligned with initialization singular vectors. All layers share balanced singular factors, training is population full-batch GD with squared loss, and zero eigenvalues are set aside. These choices isolate an architectural mechanism cleanly, yet they exclude misalignment, anisotropy, minibatch noise, nonlinear representations, residual scaling, normalization, and class structure that direct competitors analyze.

method.core_idea: Construct a whitened, aligned deep-linear learning problem in which all layer factors share singular directions, then diagonalize the outer-product Hessian to show that curvature directions supported at both ends accumulate contributions from all L layers while one-sided directions receive only one contribution.
method.mechanism: A depth-L linear map W_L...W_1 is trained by population gradient descent on squared loss. Balanced SVD initialization and a target cross-covariance aligned with the same U,V reduce the matrix dynamics to scalar singular-value recurrences. The Hessian is split into outer-product/Gauss-Newton and functional parts. The Gram matrix of the outer-product factor is diagonal in u_i tensor v_j: active-active pairs form the dominant space, active-inactive pairs form the bulk, and inactive-inactive pairs are zero within the Gram representation. Loss convergence is then invoked to make the functional term small and Weyl bounds transfer the two clusters to the full Hessian.
assumptions: The network is deep linear for the theorem, with squared population loss and full-batch gradient descent at a fixed step size.
Every hidden width is at least d_*=min(d_0,d_L).
The input covariance is a zero-padded identity on the d_* support, although appendix proofs sometimes replace that rank by r.
The target cross-covariance is U I_r V^T, exactly aligned with the singular vectors sampled at initialization and uniform only on its rank-r active subspace.
Balanced initialization factors the end-to-end SVD evenly across all L layers so their singular vectors remain shared.
For the exact two-level result, all active singular values are equal and all inactive singular values are initialized to zero.
For the stated general result, active singular values lie in a narrow interval satisfying (m+delta)/(m-delta)<L^(1/(2(L-1))).
The step size obeys eta<min(1/L,1/M^(2L-2)) and active singular values start positive.
Training proceeds long enough for the functional Hessian to be a small perturbation and active singular values to approach one.
The Gauss-Newton factorization and eigenvalue transfer are applied in the d_0<=d_L case; the reverse rectangular case is not separately proved.
Curvature associated with parameter null directions is excluded from the paper's operational definition of meaningful spectrum.
The tanh simulation is treated as suggestive evidence that the linear mechanism persists beyond the theorem.

techniques.role: Splits the full Hessian into an outer-product/Gauss-Newton term and a residual-dependent functional term.
Shares end-to-end singular directions and Lth-root singular values across all layer factors.
Reduces population GD to one-dimensional recurrences for aligned singular modes.
Diagonalizes A_o^T A_o on tensor products of left and right singular vectors.
Partitions active-active pairs into a dominant space and one-sided active pairs into a bulk space.
Produces exactly equal active singular values so the outer-product eigenvalue ratio is L.
Attempts to bound the functional Hessian by the square root of the residual loss.
Treats the functional Hessian as a perturbation of the analytically diagonalized outer-product Hessian.
Compares mean dominant and bulk eigenvalues for depths 2-7.
Repeats the small synthetic experiment with tanh activations as a nonlinear plausibility test.
Visualizes depth 2-7 spectra for ranks 4-10 in the appendix, albeit without a written protocol.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic deep linear map y=Phi x with whitened covariance/cross-covariance, input dimension 10, output dimension 16, hidden widths 20, rank 4, balanced aligned initialization; depth swept from 2 to 7.
evaluations.metric: Full Hessian eigenvalue trajectories, training loss, and mean dominant-to-bulk eigenvalue ratio.
evaluations.result: Figure 1 shows separated nonzero clusters and a plotted gap that follows the dashed Gap=L line for L=2-7; the paper does not tabulate exact gaps, seeds, or error bars.
evaluations.baseline: The theoretical ratio L under the uniform-spectrum special case; no anisotropic-data or random-initialization empirical control.

evaluations.setting: The same deep linear setup at L=3 with d_0=10, d_L=16, hidden widths 20, and r=4.
evaluations.metric: Eigenvalue trajectories, nonzero cluster multiplicities, final gap, and loss convergence.
evaluations.result: Figure 2 reports 16 dominant and 72 bulk eigenvalues, matching r^2 and (10+16-8)4, with a final mean gap near 3 and converged loss. The much larger full-parameter nullspace is not counted in the stated zero multiplicity.
evaluations.baseline: Theorem 3.5/Corollary 3.6 predictions for the aligned deep-linear special case.

evaluations.setting: Tanh activation inserted after each layer, otherwise the same small synthetic dimensions and rank; depth 2-7.
evaluations.metric: Eigenvalue trajectories, training loss, and mean dominant/bulk gap versus depth.
evaluations.result: Figure 3 visually preserves two nonzero clusters at L=3 and plots the mean gap near L across L=2-7, while dominant means grow and bulk means remain approximately constant. No numeric table, repetitions, or alternative nonlinearities are provided.

evaluations.setting: Appendix Figures 4-17, rendered from pages 28-41; legends imply ranks 4-10, each represented by one page with L=2-4 and one with L=5-7.
evaluations.metric: Hessian eigenvalue and loss trajectories, with dashed target levels for dominant, bulk, and near-zero spaces.
evaluations.result: The plots visually approach dominant level L, bulk level 1, and zero for the illustrated normalized setup. Every caption misstates panel depths as 3/4/5; the claimed dominant-plus-bulk count equals d_0 d_L only in the full-rank endpoint, not the lower-rank figures.
evaluations.baseline: Dashed theoretical levels; no documented seed, learning-rate, data-size, or nonaligned control.

limitations: [Author-stated] The theorem concerns deep linear networks; the only beyond-linear evidence is a small tanh simulation.
[Author-stated] Very large depths are not simulated because the increasingly ill-conditioned Hessian is difficult to compute numerically.
[Author-stated] Zero eigenvalues are excluded from the paper's bulk/spike definition as carrying no meaningful information.
[Reviewer-inferred] Assumption 3.1 states rank-d_* whitened covariance, while multiple appendix proofs use rank-r covariance; the two choices imply different inactive-mode dynamics.
[Reviewer-inferred] The general theorem silently needs zero inactive singular values, effectively the stronger uniform spectral initialization used only in the corollary.
[Reviewer-inferred] Nonzero inactive modes decay polynomially for L>1 and can add finite-time curvature levels that the exponential zero-space claim omits.

[Reviewer-inferred] The appendix proves the Gram spectrum explicitly only for d_*=d_0<=d_L, yet the theorem is stated symmetrically for d_*=min(d_0,d_L) and changes d_0 to d_* in the main-text bulk count.
[Reviewer-inferred] The reported zero multiplicity belongs to A_o^T A_o, not the full P-by-P parameter Hessian, whose nullity is much larger in deep networks.
[Reviewer-inferred] Corollary 3.6 overstates an asymptotic L+O(exp(-ct)) ratio as exactly L for the perturbed full Hessian.
[Reviewer-inferred] The separation threshold becomes closer to one as L grows, contrary to the claim that the condition becomes easier with depth.
[Reviewer-inferred] The stated separation condition alone does not yield uniform Theta(L) constants from the paper's own ratio bounds.
[Reviewer-inferred] The functional-Hessian proof conflates pointwise, population, and excess loss, especially when the irreducible loss is nonzero.
[Reviewer-inferred] The cross-covariance is uniform only on a rank-r aligned subspace and is rank deficient when r<d_*, so 'perfectly balanced' needs that qualifier.

[Reviewer-inferred] All empirical evidence is synthetic and tiny; no standard architecture, dataset, minibatch optimizer, residual scaling, batch/layer normalization, or classification loss is tested.
[Reviewer-inferred] Simulation pages provide no random seeds, sample count, step size, initialization distribution, repetitions, error bars, or machine-readable gap values.
[Reviewer-inferred] Appendix Figures 4-17 have incorrect depth captions and an incorrect nonzero-count statement for ranks below full rank.
failure_modes: Misalignment between target cross-covariance and initialization singular vectors destroys the shared scalar dynamics used throughout the proof.
Anisotropic or full-rank nonidentity data covariance couples modes and can create data-driven spikes on top of, or instead of, the depth mechanism.
Nonzero initialization outside target rank produces extra finite-time Hessian eigenvalues and polynomially decaying modes omitted by the stated theorem.
Unequal active singular values can violate the increasingly tight separation condition and merge the proposed dominant and bulk intervals.
At finite residual loss, an indefinite functional Hessian can shift, split, or add positive and negative eigenvalues beyond the Gauss-Newton clusters.
The parameter Hessian contains a large architecture- and symmetry-dependent nullspace that is hidden by analyzing only the d_L d_0 Gram matrix.
If d_L<d_0, the proof's B_o=I simplification fails because the zero-padded covariance is not the full d_0 identity.
Tanh saturation or other nonlinear activation derivatives can rescale layers nonuniformly and invalidate the L identical-contribution picture.
Residual branch scaling such as 1/sqrt(L) can change how curvature accumulates with depth and prevent a raw L gap.
Batch normalization or layer normalization can strongly change outlier spectra, as direct empirical predecessors show.
Minibatch noise and stochastic optimization can rotate the dominant eigenspace away from the fixed U,V basis.
Large L can make exact eigendecomposition numerically unreliable, so an apparent gap may reflect thresholding or finite precision.
Rank-deficient target moments can make the constructed 'balanced' problem unlike full-rank whitening in practical representation learning.
Caption and indexing errors can cause the appendix plots to be interpreted with the wrong depths or multiplicities.
Ignoring null directions can conceal flat symmetries that materially affect optimizer noise, parameter drift, and generalization.
reusable_insights: To show a data property is not necessary, construct an isotropic control and isolate an architectural mechanism; clearly label the result as an existence example.
Decomposing Hessian curvature into Gauss-Newton and functional terms is useful, but each term's rank, sign, and convergence rate must be tracked in the full parameter space.
Balanced deep-linear models can reduce matrix training dynamics to scalar singular-value recurrences and expose exact depth factors.
Tensor-product bases often make endpoint-supported Hessian directions analytically separable into active-active, active-inactive, and inactive-inactive classes.
Always reconcile covariance rank, target rank, and initialization rank before claiming that inactive modes are fixed or vanish.
When transferring nonzero eigenvalues through A A^T and A^T A, add the dimension-difference nullity back before describing the full spectrum.
Distinguish an exact ratio for a Gauss-Newton matrix from an asymptotic ratio for a full Hessian perturbed by residual terms.
Check how a theorem's admissible-width threshold scales with the parameter before describing a condition as easier at larger scale.
A Theta(L) claim needs constants uniform in L; a depth-dependent spread condition can otherwise hide L^2 or constant bounds.
Nonlinear boundary experiments should vary activation, residual scaling, normalization, rank, width, seeds, and real data rather than rely on one tanh plot.
Plot captions and legend index ranges are part of the scientific record and should be consistency-checked against formulas.
Report both nonzero cluster multiplicities and the complete parameter-space nullity so optimization implications are interpretable.
open_questions: Can Theorem 3.5 be restated and proved with one consistent choice of Sigma_xx rank and explicit initialization of the d_*-r modes?
What additional eigenvalue clusters arise when inactive singular values start nonzero, and at what polynomial rate do they merge into the zero space?
How should the full P-dimensional nullspace and any finite-time functional-Hessian eigenvalues be counted exactly?
Can the d_L<d_0 rectangular case be proved without the B_o=I simplification?
Under what quantitative convergence of the active singular-value spread does the general gap become uniformly Theta(L)?
Can the functional-Hessian decay be proved directly from Omega rather than conflating total and excess loss?
Does a depth-linear gap survive random, nonaligned balanced initialization at finite width?
How do residual connections with standard depth scaling, ReLU/GELU activations, and normalization change the gap law?
Can architecture-induced and class/covariance-induced spikes be additively or multiplicatively decomposed on real classifiers?
Do empirical gaps remain linear in L under minibatch SGD, Adam, or second-order preconditioning?
What optimizer design follows from the two clusters once the full nullspace and functional curvature are included?
Can the appendix rank sweep be rerun with a fully specified protocol, multiple seeds, numeric tables, and corrected captions?
Are Hessian eigenvectors in the proposed dominant space actually aligned with gradients or learning dynamics on nonlinear networks?
How sensitive are the multiplicities and gap to imperfect whitening and small U,V target misalignment?

competitive_landscape.title: Analytic Insights into Structure and Rank of Neural Network Hessian Maps
competitive_landscape.difference: Singh, Bachmann, and Hofmann derive exact formulas and tight rank bounds for deep-linear Hessians and validate numerical rank on ReLU and tanh networks; the target directly uses their outer-product factorization. The target's additional objective is eigenvalue magnitude, specifically a two-level spectrum and depth-L gap under whitened aligned balanced dynamics, rather than rank deficiency alone.
competitive_landscape.source_version: NeurIPS 2021 publisher record, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34

competitive_landscape.title: Theoretical Characterisation of the Gauss Newton Conditioning in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhao, Singh, and Lucchi give tight Gauss-Newton condition-number bounds for deep linear networks of arbitrary depth and width and extend analysis to two-layer ReLU, residual, and convolutional architectures. The target narrows to an aligned isotropic deep-linear trajectory and claims exact cluster multiplicities and an L gap for the full Hessian after the functional term decays.
competitive_landscape.source_version: NeurIPS 2024 Main Conference, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37, DOI 10.52202/079017-3650

competitive_landscape.title: A Convergence Analysis of Gradient Descent for Deep Linear Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Arora, Cohen, Golowich, and Hu prove linear convergence for deep-linear squared loss over whitened data under sufficient width, approximately balanced initialization, and an initial-loss condition. The target adopts that balanced/whitened framework and singular-factor dynamics, then studies Hessian clusters; its additional Hessian theorem therefore depends on a highly inherited optimization setup rather than introducing the setup itself.
competitive_landscape.source_version: ICLR 2019 published OpenReview version, forum SkMQg3C5K7

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Linear Network Training Dynamics from Random Initialization: Data, Width, Depth, and Hyperparameter Transfer
competitive_landscape.difference: Bordelon and Pehlevan analyze large-width deep-linear training from random initialization with random data, width/depth effects, parameterization, stochastic versus repeated data, and residual networks with an infinite-depth scaling. The target gives a finite-width exact Hessian spectrum in a much more aligned deterministic setting, but does not address the random, residual, or hyperparameter-transfer regimes that can alter depth scaling.

competitive_landscape.title: An Investigation into Neural Net Optimization via Hessian Eigenvalue Density
competitive_landscape.difference: Ghorbani, Krishnan, and Xiao measure full Hessian densities through training at ImageNet scale, observe rapid isolated eigenvalues and gradient concentration, and show those effects are nearly absent with batch normalization. The target provides a synthetic analytic depth mechanism under whitened data, but does not test normalization or establish that its L-gap mechanism explains the empirical outliers in modern networks.

competitive_landscape.title: Traces of Class/Cross-Class Structure Pervade Deep Learning Spectra
competitive_landscape.difference: Papyan formally attributes outliers, spikes, bumps, and other spectral structure in classifiers to class and cross-class components. The target supplies a complementary existence example in which an active data covariance is isotropic and depth alone creates two Gauss-Newton levels; it does not refute class structure as an explanation in real classification or study how the two mechanisms combine.

competitive_landscape.title: Geometry of Neural Network Loss Surfaces via Random Matrix Theory
competitive_landscape.difference: Pennington and Bahri approximate Hessian spectral densities at critical points with random matrix theory and show dependence on loss energy and the parameter-to-data ratio. The target instead obtains discrete exact levels for a deterministic aligned deep-linear model near convergence and emphasizes depth rather than random spectral density; its result covers a narrower but more algebraically explicit regime.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim to show for the first time that Hessian bulk-and-spike bifurcation does not require imbalanced data: in a whitened deep-linear model, architecture alone yields r^2 dominant directions, a lower bulk, and a dominant-to-bulk gap that grows linearly and, under uniform spectral initialization, exactly equals depth L.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper derives shared factor dynamics, diagonalizes the outer-product Hessian in a singular-vector Kronecker basis, bounds a functional-Hessian perturbation, and plots small deep-linear and tanh spectra for depths 2-7 and apparent ranks 4-10. The uniform-zero-inactive special case does yield two nonzero Gauss-Newton levels with an exact L ratio and therefore supplies a legitimate architecture-only existence construction.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Prior work already derives deep-linear Hessian rank structure, depth/architecture-dependent Gauss-Newton conditioning, balanced deep-linear dynamics, and empirical/class-structured bulk-and-outlier spectra. The most defensible novelty is the explicit active-pair versus one-sided-pair eigenvalue calculation showing an L ratio under isotropic active covariance, aligned rank-r target, and uniform rank-r factors. The broad general theorem and full-spectrum language are not established as written: covariance rank changes inside the proof, inactive modes alternate between fixed and decaying, Lemma A.9 assumes zeros not required by the theorem, the nullspace count is for the smaller Gram matrix, and finite-time exact-L/Theta(L) statements are overstated. The result therefore supports 'data imbalance is not necessary in this constructed special case,' not 'depth generally explains observed DNN spikes.'

verification.passage_check: Read and second-pass checked all 41 cached pages in order, including every main-text definition, assumption, theorem, equation, reference, Lemmas A.1-A.11, both restated main results, and the complete simulation appendix. PDF pages 28-41 were rendered and visually inspected because extraction contains mostly captions; legend multiplicities, actual L=2-7 panel labels, repeated caption errors, and rank progression were checked. Scalar recurrences, covariance ranks, separation bounds, Gram/full-Hessian dimensions, and the main L=3 parameter count were independently audited, with author claims separated from proof contradictions and reviewer generalization boundaries.

Titles, fixed proceedings versions, abstracts, mathematical scope, empirical regime, and concrete relationship to the target were checked; the target was excluded.

reviewer_notes: The indexed PDF and text hashes match fulltext_index exactly, all 41 pages are present, and the official arXiv record identifies the cached current paper as v3 revised 2026-05-24. The mathematical audit distinguishes a credible uniform-rank outer-product special case from the unverified general/full-Hessian theorem. The L=3 nullity calculation uses the paper's own dimensions: 920 parameters and 88 predicted nonzero outer-product eigenvalues imply 832 null directions, whereas 72 is only the zero count of the 160-dimensional end-to-end Gram representation. Figures 4-17 contain no explanatory text beyond repeated captions; rank values are inferred from their explicit legend index ranges and formulas, and that inference is labeled accordingly. Remaining uncertainty concerns whether a corrected manuscript or code repository imposes zero inactive initialization and a consistent covariance rank, neither of which is stated in this PDF's general theorem.
